tagline.text: Asia's steel Gothic church, shipped from Belgium by boat and assembled on site

children.text: A neo-Gothic church assembled from prefabricated steel parts shipped from Belgium in the late 19th century — the only steel church in the Philippines and a national cultural treasure. Its twin spires, steel columns painted to look like marble, and German stained glass reveal a quiet beauty amid the bustle of Quiapo.

San Sebastian Church is a minor basilica standing before Plaza del Carmen, east of Manila's Quiapo district. It is run by the Augustinian Recollects, whose San Sebastian College sits right beside it. The first church here was built after a devotee of Saint Sebastian donated the land in
, but the wood-and-brick churches that followed collapsed repeatedly to fire and earthquakes.
After a major earthquake brought down the fourth church in

, the Recollects decided to rebuild it in steel, resistant to both fire and earthquakes. Spanish architect Genaro Palacios designed it, and about 52 tons of prefabricated steel parts arrived from Belgium in eight shipments. The parts carried numbers marking the assembly order, and the church was consecrated on
August 16, 1891
, roughly a year after the first column went up in
. A widespread story credits Gustave Eiffel, builder of the Eiffel Tower, with a role in the design, but no record supports it.

The church rises on a steel frame in an earthquake baroque and neo-Gothic style, striking for its two sky-piercing spires and pale turquoise-toned facade. It was declared a National Historical Landmark in
and a national cultural treasure in
, and was once on the UNESCO World Heritage tentative list. However, sea air and humidity have caused serious corrosion of the steel, and phased conservation work has continued in recent years.

Where Quiapo Church is a crowded, fervent center of worship, San Sebastian is a place to quietly take in architecture and light. It's especially worth recommending to travelers who love architecture and photography, or anyone who wants to tour Manila's old churches like a pilgrimage, and it pairs well with Quiapo Church on foot for a half-day itinerary.

blocks.title: See the church built entirely of steel

children.text: The walls, columns, and even the ceiling are all prefabricated steel. From a distance it looks like stone or wood, but up close the joints and rivets show through. It's a rare building where you can see late-19th-century prefabricated construction with your own eyes.

blocks.title: Admire the twin spires and facade

children.text: Looking up from Plaza del Carmen, the two pointed spires and the rose window fit into a single frame. In the morning, sunlight hits the facade directly for sharper photos.

blocks.title: Columns and ceiling painted to look like marble

children.text: Inside, the steel columns and vaulted ceiling were painted by Filipino artists to resemble marble and wood grain. The central nave, where the tall Gothic arches meet the chandeliers, looks most magnificent when viewed from the back toward the altar.
The stained glass filling the windows was made at the Heinrich Oidtmann workshop in Germany. Visit at midday when the sun is high to see the colored light spill across the steel columns.

blocks.title: Our Lady of Mount Carmel statue

children.text: Sent by the Discalced Carmelite nuns of Mexico around
, this is the oldest documented image of Our Lady of Mount Carmel in the Philippines. It is said to have survived several fires and earthquakes, was canonically crowned with Vatican approval in
, and now stands at the center of the altar.

blocks.title: Spot the assembly numbers on the ceiling

children.text: Identification marks left over from when the parts were made in Belgium remain visible on parts of the ceiling and columns. Ask a church caretaker or check the information panels for their location to bring the construction story to life.

blocks.title: Plaza del Carmen and the Dung-aw ritual

children.text: The small plaza in front of the church is where the Traslacion procession passes on
January 9
. On this day, the Our Lady of Mount Carmel statue and the Black Nazarene face each other in the "Dung-aw" ritual, drawing large crowds of the faithful.

blocks.title: Watch the conservation work in progress

children.text: Conservation work to replace rusted steel and restore the paintwork is proceeding in phases, so some areas may have scaffolding up. Information panels inside the church explain the restoration process, and you can contribute to the restoration fund through the donation box.

Manila is easiest to visit during the
December–April
dry season. The high ceiling keeps the church interior relatively cool, but there's no air conditioning, so visit in the morning during
April–May
, when temperatures climb to
June–October
is the rainy and typhoon season, and heavy rain can flood the streets around Quiapo and Legarda.
The church's biggest feast day is Our Lady of Mount Carmel on
July 16
, with processions and masses around it. The feast of Saint Sebastian falls on
January 20
, and during the Traslacion on
January 9

, the procession passes in front of the church and the area fills with crowds. For the best view of the stained glass, visit at midday on a clear day when the sun is high, and note that weddings are often held on weekend afternoons, which can limit interior viewing.

The area around the church, a university district and working-class neighborhood, has almost no traveler lodging. If you're combining it with an Old Manila tour, it's convenient to stay at a business hotel in Binondo (about
per night) or a hotel in Ermita/Malate near Manila Bay (about
) and travel by LRT or Grab. A half-day trip from Quezon City or Makati also works well.

The area around the church sits in the "U-Belt," home to San Sebastian College and other universities, so cheap eateries catering to students are plentiful. A carinderia meal of rice with one or two viands costs about

, and street food like fish balls, kwek-kwek (fried quail eggs), and buko juice is easy to find. The Muslim quarter near Quiapo, a short walk away, serves halal food, and a bit farther on, Binondo's Chinatown offers dumplings and noodles. For a proper sit-down meal, it's best to head to Binondo or Intramuros after visiting.
Weekdays outside Mass hours, roughly
9 AM–4 PM
, are the best time to visit. Opening hours can change due to conservation work and events, so check the official Facebook page for the latest notices.
Weddings are frequently held on weekend afternoons and holidays. During a ceremony, watch quietly from the back or wait until it ends.
Use a wide-angle lens or your phone's wide mode to fit the whole church in one shot. The plaza is narrow, making it hard to capture both spires.
Some visitors tap the columns to hear the metal ring, but please don't touch or tap them, to protect the paintwork and the heritage structure.
Avoid sleeveless tops and short shorts, and take off your hat inside the church.
Combine Quiapo Church, San Sebastian Church, Binondo Church, and San Agustin Church in Intramuros into a single day for an old-churches pilgrimage route through Manila.
During conservation work, some areas may be roped off or have scaffolding up. Don't enter areas marked off-limits, and check official notices before visiting to confirm what's open.
The area around Quiapo and Legarda station is crowded and pickpocketing is common. Wear your bag in front and don't walk with your phone in your hand.
Avoid flash photography and moving near the altar during Mass; take photos only when there's no service in progress.
On Traslacion day, the area around the church is extremely crowded and roads are closed. It's best to avoid visiting that day.
After dark, the streets around the church become dim and quiet. In the evening, call a Grab from a main road.
